stages.title: DAW Basics and Signal Flow
stages.description: How a DAW session is organised: audio vs MIDI tracks, instruments that turn MIDI into sound, and how signals flow through group, return and main tracks.
learningObjectives: Explain the difference between audio tracks and MIDI tracks
Describe how a software instrument turns MIDI data into audio
Trace a track's signal to the main (master) output using input/output routing
Use group tracks (buses) and return tracks fed by sends

explainBack.question: What is the difference between a MIDI track and an audio track, and how does sound travel from a track to the speakers in a DAW?
rubric: Audio tracks hold recorded sound (audio is sound); MIDI holds performance data such as which notes, how long and velocity, and contains no sound itself
A software instrument on a MIDI track converts MIDI into audio, so MIDI parts can still be edited non-destructively (transpose, quantize, swap the instrument)
Every track's output is routed (via its input/output routing choosers) to the Main/master track by default
Group tracks sum several tracks into one bus/submix that has its own mixer controls and can host effects
Return tracks receive signal from the send controls on other tracks, so one effect can be shared by many tracks

resources.title: AUDIO vs MIDI - What's the difference??
resources.description: A short explainer contrasting audio recordings with MIDI note data inside a DAW.
keyPoints: Compares audio and MIDI as two kinds of track content
Explains why MIDI parts stay editable
Aimed at producers new to DAWs

resources.title: Beginner's Guide: MIDI vs Audio
resources.author: E.M.M.A.
resources.description: Explains that audio is sound while MIDI is performance data that tells instruments what to play, and lists what that means for editing.
keyPoints: Audio is sound; a MIDI signal contains no sound
MIDI stores which notes were played, their length and velocity
MIDI edits are non-destructive: change instrument, quantize, transpose
MIDI cables carry only data, so hardware synths also need audio cables
MIDI has 16 channels for addressing multiple instruments

resources.title: Routing and I/O
resources.description: The official Live manual chapter on how tracks get their input and where they send their output, including sends, returns and group routing.
keyPoints: Audio tracks have an audio input; MIDI tracks have a MIDI input
Instruments convert MIDI to audio
The track In/Out section acts as a patchbay for sources and destinations
Return tracks receive their input from the corresponding sends

resources.title: Mixing
resources.description: Describes Live's mixer: audio/MIDI tracks, group tracks as summing containers, return tracks for shared effects, and the Main track as the default destination.
keyPoints: The Main track is the default destination for all other tracks
Group Tracks sum tracks, have mixer controls and can host audio effects
Return tracks process audio sent from many tracks via Send controls
Mixer controls include volume, pan, mute (Track Activator), solo and arm

stages.title: Rhythm and Drum Programming
stages.description: Programming drum patterns on a grid: tempo in BPM, beats and bars, time signatures, common kick/snare patterns, quantization and velocity.
learningObjectives: Explain tempo (BPM) and how it relates to genre
Read a time signature and relate beats to bars
Program a four-on-the-floor kick with a backbeat
Use quantization and velocity to control timing and dynamics

explainBack.question: How would you program a basic house-style drum beat in a DAW, and how do tempo, time signature, quantization and velocity affect it?
rubric: Tempo is measured in beats per minute (BPM) and helps define genre, e.g. house roughly 115-130 BPM vs drum and bass roughly 160-180 BPM
In a time signature the top number is the number of beats per bar and the bottom number is the note value that gets the beat; 4/4 = four quarter-note beats per bar
A four-on-the-floor pattern puts the kick on every beat (steps 1, 5, 9, 13 of a 16-step bar); a backbeat puts the snare or clap on beats 2 and 4
Quantizing moves MIDI notes onto the grid; a quantize Amount below 100% moves notes only part of the way to keep a less mechanical feel
Velocity sets how loud/hard each note plays, and varying it adds dynamics to a pattern

resources.title: Make your first beat in Ableton Live | Beginner Series Ep. 1
resources.description: Ableton's beginner series episode on building a first beat from MIDI drum patterns and audio loops.
keyPoints: Builds a beat from MIDI drum patterns
Combines programmed drums with audio loops
First episode of Ableton's official beginner series

resources.title: Beat and Tempo
resources.description: Interactive lesson defining the beat as a steady pulse and tempo as its speed in beats per minute, with a four-on-the-floor exercise.
keyPoints: A beat can mean a drum pattern or the steady underlying pulse
Tempo is measured in beats per minute (BPM)
Kick notes at steps 1, 5, 9 and 13 make a four-on-the-floor pattern

resources.title: Tempo and Genre
resources.description: Shows how changing tempo changes the feel of the same pattern and lists typical BPM ranges for common genres.
keyPoints: Genre depends on sounds, patterns and tempo
House is about 115-130 BPM; techno/trance about 120-140
Hip-hop about 60-100 BPM; drum and bass about 160-180

resources.title: Backbeats
resources.description: Interactive lesson combining a four-on-the-floor kick with claps or snares on beats 2 and 4.
keyPoints: A backbeat is a clap or snare on the second and fourth beats
Four-on-the-floor places the kick on every beat
The combination is common in techno and house

resources.title: Simple Meter and Time Signatures
resources.description: Open textbook chapter explaining what each number in a time signature means, with common examples.
keyPoints: Top number: how many beats are in each measure
Bottom number: which note value gets the beat (4 = quarter note)
4/4 has four quarter-note beats per measure; 3/4 has three
A time signature is not a fraction

resources.title: Editing MIDI
resources.description: Official manual chapter on editing MIDI notes, including the grid, quantizing and velocity editing.
keyPoints: Quantizing aligns notes to the grid; Ctrl/Cmd+U quantizes selected notes
The Amount control moves notes only a percentage of the way to the grid
Velocity represents note loudness and is shown by note colour
Velocities can be drawn, ramped, randomized or given deviation

stages.title: Music Theory for Producers
stages.description: The theory you need to write parts in a piano roll: keys and scales, building major and minor triads, and reading chord progressions in Roman numerals.
learningObjectives: Explain what a key, tonic and scale are
Build a major scale from its whole/half-step pattern
Build major and minor triads from a scale
Read and use a Roman-numeral chord progression such as I-V-vi-IV

explainBack.question: How would you pick notes and chords for a song in C major, and what makes a chord major or minor?
rubric: A key centres on a tonic ('home' note); a scale is the set of notes used, e.g. C major has no sharps or flats
A major scale follows the step pattern whole-whole-half-whole-whole-whole-half
A triad stacks the 3rd and 5th scale notes above a root: C major = C-E-G, C minor = C-Eb-G
Major triads tend to sound bright/happy and minor triads dark/sad
Progressions are written with Roman numerals for scale degrees; I-V-vi-IV underpins hundreds of pop songs

resources.title: Write a chord progression in Ableton Live | Beginner Series Ep. 2
resources.description: Ableton's beginner series episode on writing a chord progression for a track.
keyPoints: Writes chords in a DAW piano roll
Builds a progression to sit with the drums from episode 1
Part of Ableton's official beginner series

resources.title: Keys and Scales
resources.description: Interactive lesson introducing the tonic, keys and scales as a palette of notes.
keyPoints: A key has a tonic, the most stable 'home' note
A scale is an ordered subset of notes, like a palette
Major scales are usually heard as bright; minor as darker

resources.title: Building Major Scales
resources.description: Lesson showing that every major scale uses the same pattern of whole and half steps from any tonic.
keyPoints: Major scales have seven notes before the octave
Pattern: whole-whole-half-whole-whole-whole-half
Each letter name appears once per scale
C major is the only major scale with no sharps or flats

resources.title: Major Triads
resources.description: Lesson building triads by adding the third and fifth scale notes above a root.
keyPoints: Triads add the 3rd and 5th scale notes above a root
The C major triad is C, E and G
Major triads are usually heard as happy or uplifting

resources.title: Minor Triads
resources.description: Lesson building minor triads from the minor scale, contrasting them with major triads.
keyPoints: The C minor triad is C, Eb and G
Built from the 1st, 3rd and 5th notes of the minor scale
Minor triads are usually heard as sad or dark

resources.description: Lesson on the I-V-vi-IV progression and how many pop songs share it.
keyPoints: I-V-vi-IV forms the basis of hundreds of pop songs
Demonstrated in D major
Invites rearranging chords to hear tension and resolution

stages.title: Recording Audio at Home
stages.description: Capturing clean recordings: setting input gain, choosing sample rate and bit depth, managing latency with buffer size, and placing a microphone.
learningObjectives: Set input gain to get a healthy level without clipping
Choose a sample rate and bit depth and explain what each controls
Adjust buffer size to balance latency against CPU load
Place a vocal microphone with awareness of proximity effect and room sound

explainBack.question: You're about to record vocals at home. How do you set up levels, session format, latency and the mic?
rubric: Sets input gain for a healthy signal above the noise floor without clipping; at 24-bit you can leave generous headroom (e.g. averages around -18 dBFS rather than peaks near 0)
Sample rate sets the highest recordable frequency (about half the sample rate), so 44.1/48 kHz covers the ~20 kHz hearing range; 48 kHz at 24-bit is a common choice
Each bit adds about 6 dB of dynamic range: 16-bit about 96 dB, 24-bit about 144 dB, so 24-bit lowers the noise floor
Smaller buffer sizes give lower latency but use more CPU and can cause dropouts; larger buffers are more stable but add latency
Close miking gives a drier sound with less room but very close placement adds bass (proximity effect); room sound captured at a distance cannot be removed later

resources.title: Everything you need to record vocals at home (Logic Pro X, Garageband, Ableton, Etc..)
resources.description: Walkthrough of a home vocal recording setup: mic, shock mount, pop shield, cable and connecting to a DAW.
keyPoints: Explains each piece of a vocal recording kit
Shows assembling and connecting a condenser mic
Applies to any interface and DAW

resources.title: Q. Should I gain-stage to -6dBFS or -18dBFS?
resources.author: Matt Houghton
resources.description: Explains recording vs mixing level targets: aim for a healthy signal without clipping, and why 24-bit allows more headroom.
keyPoints: When recording, aim for a healthy level relative to noise without clipping
At 24-bit the noise floor is low enough to leave plenty of headroom
-18 dBFS refers to average (RMS) level, not peaks
Floating-point DAW mixers can't clip internally, but the output must stay under 0 dBFS

resources.title: Gain staging: what it is and how to do it
resources.author: Nick Messitte
resources.description: Defines gain staging as keeping each stage at an optimal level to minimise noise and distortion, with -18 dBFS as a common reference.
keyPoints: Gain staging balances noise floor against distortion
About -18 dBFS is a common calibration level; some use -20
Exported files must stay below 0 dBFS to avoid permanent clipping

resources.title: Digital audio basics: audio sample rate and bit depth
resources.author: Ian Stewart
resources.description: Explains how sample rate limits the highest frequency and how bit depth sets the noise floor and dynamic range.
keyPoints: Recording frequency f needs a sample rate of at least 2f
Each bit adds about 6 dB: 16-bit ~96 dB, 24-bit ~144 dB
48 or 96 kHz at 24-bit suits most music production
Higher sample rates don't make low frequencies 'smoother'

resources.title: How to reduce latency
resources.description: Official support article on audio buffer size, sample rate, drivers and plug-in latency.
keyPoints: Audio is processed in parcels of time called buffers
Smaller buffers lower latency but use more CPU and risk dropouts
Use ASIO drivers on Windows and avoid Bluetooth/Wi-Fi audio
Some plug-ins add latency; delay compensation keeps tracks in sync

resources.title: Q. At what distance from my mic should I record my voice?
resources.author: Sam Inglis
resources.description: Compares close and distant vocal miking, covering proximity effect, room sound, low-cut filters and polar patterns.
keyPoints: Close miking gives a dry vocal you can add reverb to later
Very close placement sounds artificially bassy (proximity effect)
Farther away captures room reverb and noise you can't remove later
Cardioid favours the front; omni picks up all directions

stages.title: Synthesis Basics
stages.description: How a subtractive synth makes sound: oscillators and waveforms, filters, ADSR envelopes and LFO modulation.
learningObjectives: Describe common oscillator waveforms and their tone
Use a filter's cutoff and resonance to shape tone
Shape a sound over time with an ADSR envelope
Use an LFO to add movement (vibrato, tremolo, filter sweeps)

explainBack.question: Explain how you would design a simple synth bass or pad using an oscillator, filter, envelope and LFO.
rubric: The oscillator generates the raw waveform: sine is the purest, sawtooth contains all harmonics and is bright, square is edgy/hollow, triangle is soft
Subtractive synthesis starts from a harmonically rich wave and filters it: a low-pass filter removes frequencies above the cutoff and resonance boosts frequencies around the cutoff
ADSR: attack is time to reach peak, decay is time to fall to the sustain level, sustain is a level held while the key is down, release is the fade time after the key is released
An LFO is a sub-audio oscillator that modulates another parameter: on pitch it gives vibrato, on amplitude tremolo, on filter cutoff a wah/sweep

resources.title: Synthesizer Tutorial for Beginners // Synth Programming 101
resources.description: Beginner synth programming tutorial covering oscillators, filters, envelopes and LFOs, then building bass, acid and pad sounds.
keyPoints: Covers the shared building blocks of most synths
Explains oscillators, filters and envelopes
Demonstrates LFO modulation and example patches

resources.title: Learning Synths: Get Started
resources.description: Browser-based interactive synth from Ableton with lessons on oscillators, filter, envelopes and LFO.
keyPoints: Play a synth in the browser and learn its parts
Lessons on oscillators, filter, envelopes and LFO
Requires JavaScript in a modern browser

resources.title: Soft Synth Essentials: Oscillators, Envelopes, and Filters
resources.author: Josh Kipersztok
resources.description: Introduces oscillator waveforms, ADSR envelopes, filter types with resonance, and LFOs in software synths.
keyPoints: Sawtooth contains all harmonic overtones and sounds bright
Triangle is softer, closer to a sine; square is edgy
Low-pass removes highs, high-pass removes lows, band-pass keeps the middle
Resonance emphasises the level at the cutoff

resources.title: Analog Synthesizer Basics: Oscillators, Filters, Envelopes, More
resources.author: Gabby Bloch
resources.description: Overview of the main subtractive-synth sections: oscillators, filters with cutoff and resonance, ADSR envelopes and LFOs.
keyPoints: Oscillators produce sine, square, sawtooth and triangle waves
Subtractive synthesis shapes sound by removing harmonic content
Cutoff sets where filtering happens; resonance emphasises it
LFOs run below hearing range to modulate other parameters

resources.title: ADSR envelopes
resources.description: University course notes defining the four ADSR stages and how note-on and note-off trigger them.
keyPoints: Attack rises to peak; decay falls to the sustain level
Sustain is a level, not a time
Release starts at note-off and falls to zero
Envelopes can control gain, brightness, vibrato and more

resources.title: Chapter 11: A Basic Synthesis Model
resources.author: Dan Hosken
resources.description: Companion page to a music-technology textbook presenting the oscillator-filter-amplifier model with envelope and LFO modulation examples.
keyPoints: Model: oscillator, filter, amplifier with envelope, modulation
LFO on pitch creates vibrato; on amplitude, tremolo
Modulating filter cutoff gives wah-like sweeps
Also covers PWM, detuning, ring modulation and sync

stages.title: Mixing Fundamentals
stages.description: Balancing a mix with levels and panning, shaping tone with EQ, controlling dynamics with compression, and adding space with reverb and delay on send/return tracks.
learningObjectives: Balance levels and position sounds with panning
Use EQ filters to remove problems and separate instruments
Set a compressor's threshold, ratio, attack, release and makeup gain
Apply reverb and delay through sends and return tracks

explainBack.question: Walk through how you'd mix a simple track: balance, EQ, compression and reverb.
rubric: Volume faders set each track's level and pan positions its output in the stereo field
EQ boosts or cuts frequencies: high-pass filters remove unwanted lows, bell filters have frequency, gain and Q, and EQ is judged in context of the whole mix

Compression reduces gain above the threshold by the ratio (at 3:1, 3 dB over the threshold comes out as 1 dB over); attack/release set how fast it reacts and recovers, and makeup/output gain restores level
Reverb/delay go on a return (aux) track fed by sends, the return effect is set 100% wet, and each track's send level sets how much effect it gets
More reverb pushes a sound further back in the mix; less brings it forward

resources.title: Mix and automate your track in Ableton Live | Beginner Series Ep. 7
resources.description: Ableton's beginner series episode on mixing a track and adding automation.
keyPoints: Balances a finished arrangement in the mixer
Applies effects while mixing
Introduces automation for mix moves

resources.title: Mixing
resources.description: Official chapter on the mixer: volume, pan, meters, sends, return tracks with pre/post options, and group tracks.
keyPoints: Pan positions a track's output in the stereo field
Meters show peak and RMS levels
Send controls set how much of a track feeds a return track
Pre/Post toggles tap the send before or after the volume/pan stage

resources.title: Introduction to EQ
resources.author: Maarten de Boer
resources.description: Introduces EQ filter types (high/low pass, shelf, bell) and three uses: removing problems, balancing instruments and enhancing character.
keyPoints: High-pass (low cut) removes lows; low-pass (high cut) removes highs
Bell filters have frequency, gain and Q (bandwidth)
Shelves suit broad tonal changes
Always EQ sounds in context, not in isolation

resources.title: Live Audio Effect Reference
resources.description: Official reference for Live's audio effects; the Compressor section defines threshold, ratio, attack, release and output gain.
keyPoints: Threshold sets where compression begins
Ratio 3: 3 dB more input above threshold gives only 1 dB more output
Attack: time to reach full compression; release: time to recover
Output gain restores level after compression reduces peaks

resources.title: What is Reverb in Music?
resources.author: Erik Hawkins
resources.description: Berklee instructor's guide to using one bus reverb across a mix, at 100% wet, to create depth.
keyPoints: Put reverb on a bus and send each track to it
Keep the reverb's dry/wet at 100% processed
Control the amount per track with its send level
More reverb pushes a part back; less brings it forward

stages.title: Arrangement and Song Structure
stages.description: Turning a loop into a full track: song sections and their jobs, common forms, building tension into a drop, and using automation to shape energy.
learningObjectives: Organise a track into sections built from 4/8/16-bar blocks
Explain the roles of intro, verse, pre-chorus, chorus, bridge and outro
Build tension into a drop or chorus with build-up techniques
Record or draw automation to change parameters over time

explainBack.question: How would you turn an 8-bar loop into a complete song with a satisfying structure and energy curve?
rubric: Sections are built from patterns that repeat in multiples of 4, 8 or 16 bars and then combined (arranging)
A verse repeats its music with new lyrics; a chorus repeats the same lyrics and hook and is the peak; a pre-chorus builds into it; a bridge contrasts and usually comes once, after the second chorus
A common pop form is intro, verse, pre-chorus, chorus, verse, pre-chorus, chorus, bridge, chorus, (outro)

A build-up creates tension before a drop using automation such as filter sweeps/high-passing, risers, pitch rises and accelerating snare rolls, reduced bass, and often a brief silence; 8 bars is a common length
Automation records or draws a parameter's movement over the timeline (e.g. with Automation Arm or by drawing breakpoints)

resources.title: Turn your loop into a track in Ableton Live | Beginner Series Ep. 5
resources.description: Ableton's beginner series episode on arranging a loop into a full track.
keyPoints: Expands a loop into song sections
Shows arranging in the Arrangement timeline
Part of Ableton's official beginner series

resources.title: Song Structure
resources.description: Interactive lesson on how songs are built from smaller blocks of time combined into sections.
keyPoints: A song is a block of time broken into smaller blocks
Patterns usually repeat in multiples of 4, 8 or 16 bars
Arranging means combining sections into a full piece

resources.title: Song structure
resources.description: Encyclopedia overview of the standard sections of popular songs and the most common verse-chorus layouts.
keyPoints: Verse music returns with new lyrics each time
Chorus keeps the same lyrics and carries the hook
Pre-chorus builds toward the chorus; bridge contrasts, often after chorus 2
Common form: intro, verse, pre-chorus, chorus, verse, pre-chorus, chorus, bridge, chorus

resources.title: How to Write a Bridge to a Song
resources.author: Andrea Stolpe
resources.description: Berklee songwriting instructor explains where the bridge falls in a typical song and how it creates musical and lyrical contrast.
keyPoints: Bridge usually appears after the second chorus
Bridges give musical contrast: new chords, dynamics, melody or rhythm
A bridge can extend or exceed the second chorus's high point

resources.title: The Ultimate Guide to Build-ups
resources.author: Sam Matla
resources.description: Guide to building tension before a drop in electronic music using automation, risers, snare rolls and contrast.
keyPoints: Build-ups create tension that makes the drop hit harder
Automation (filter sweeps, reverb, pitch) is the main tool
Snare rolls that speed up and risers signal the change
8 bars is a reliable build-up length; silence before a drop adds contrast

resources.title: Automation and Editing Envelopes
resources.description: Official chapter on recording automation with Automation Arm and drawing or editing automation envelopes.
keyPoints: Automation is a control's movement along the timeline
Enable Automation Arm to record control changes
Draw and edit breakpoints in Automation Mode
Re-Enable Automation restores overridden automation

stages.title: Mastering and Delivery
stages.description: Finishing a track for release: measuring loudness in LUFS, limiting, true-peak headroom, streaming normalization and exporting the right file format.
learningObjectives: Measure loudness with LUFS (integrated, short-term, momentary)
Explain how streaming services normalize loudness
Use a limiter and set a true-peak ceiling
Export a master in an appropriate format, bit depth and dither

explainBack.question: How would you prepare and export a finished track for Spotify and other streaming services?
rubric: LUFS measures perceived loudness; integrated LUFS is the average over the whole song (used by streaming services), short-term uses a 3 s window and momentary 400 ms
Streaming services normalize playback: Spotify's default is -14 LUFS (louder tracks turned down, quieter ones turned up), Apple Music about -16 and YouTube about -14
A limiter is a brick-wall, high-ratio compressor that stops peaks exceeding a set ceiling and is used to raise loudness; over-limiting causes distortion and dulled transients
Spotify recommends keeping true peak below -1 dBTP, or below -2 dBTP if the master is louder than -14 LUFS, because inter-sample peaks can distort after lossy encoding
Export the master as lossless WAV/AIFF/FLAC (24-bit, or 16-bit with dither); dither is applied only once, on the final reduction in bit depth

resources.title: LUFS Explained – SIMPLE! (Mastering for Spotify)
resources.description: Short explainer on LUFS and how loudness targets apply when mastering for Spotify.
keyPoints: Explains what LUFS measures
Relates LUFS to Spotify's loudness normalization
Aimed at producers mastering their own music

resources.title: What are LUFS? The complete guide
resources.description: Explains LUFS and the momentary, short-term, integrated, loudness-range and true-peak readings on a loudness meter.
keyPoints: LUFS = loudness units relative to full scale, K-weighted
Momentary uses a 400 ms window; short-term a 3 s window
Integrated is the average over the whole song
True peak uses oversampling to catch peaks between samples

resources.title: Loudness normalization on Spotify
resources.description: Spotify's official explanation of its loudness normalization targets, limiter behaviour and true-peak recommendations.
keyPoints: Default normalization is -14 LUFS (ITU 1770)
Loud setting is -11 LUFS, Quiet is -19 LUFS
Keep masters below -1 dBTP; below -2 dBTP if louder than -14 LUFS
Albums are normalized as a whole to keep relative levels

resources.title: How to master for streaming platforms: normalization, LUFS, and loudness
resources.author: Ian Stewart
resources.description: Explains loudness normalization across platforms and why it is a listener convenience rather than a mastering target.
keyPoints: Spotify -14, Apple Music -16, YouTube -14, Deezer -15 LUFS
Normalization exists so listeners don't keep adjusting volume
Keep true peaks around -1 dBTP to avoid codec distortion
Master for the best sound, not a number

resources.title: An introduction to limiters (and how to use them)
resources.author: Nick Messitte
resources.description: Explains what a limiter does in mastering, its ceiling, gain and release controls, true-peak modes and signs of over-limiting.
keyPoints: A limiter applies brick-wall compression to stop peaks passing the ceiling
Mastering ceilings are typically set between -1.0 and -0.1 dBFS
True-peak modes catch peaks between samples
Over-limiting causes distortion, dull transients and lost groove

resources.title: Managing Files and Sets
resources.description: Official chapter including audio export: file types, sample rate conversion, bit depth and dither options.
keyPoints: Exports WAV, AIFF and FLAC, plus MP3 at 320 kbps CBR
Bit depth options are 16, 24 or 32-bit
Dither should be applied only once to any file
Export at 32-bit if more processing will follow

name: Music Production
description: Make music at home in a DAW, from tracks, beats and basic theory through recording, synthesis, mixing, arrangement and mastering for streaming.
